items.originalTitle: Gemini Omni 1.1 Flash lets you build with more control
items.summary:
Google DeepMind has launched Gemini Omni 1.1 Flash, an update to its generative video model that offers developers improved control over video creation. The new features include the ability to extend scenes up to 40 seconds with better visual consistency, specify start and end frames for smooth transitions, and upscale videos to 4K resolution. Developers can access the model through Google AI Studio or the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform.

The update also introduces faster prototyping with 360p previews to reduce costs during iteration. Gemini Omni 1.1 Flash supports real-world reasoning for generative video workflows, enabling longer storytelling and professional-quality video production. These enhancements aim to make generative video tools more practical for creative and media editing applications.

He also shares insights from conversations with investors and entrepreneurs, emphasizing that the high cost of AI inference has hindered consumer AI product development. Calvin believes that small models will enable new business use cases by providing responsive, cost-effective AI assistance for everyday work, such as managing communications and workflows. He notes that further development is needed to ensure safety and usability in business contexts but expresses confidence in progress toward these goals.

items.originalTitle: How much of a problem is AI’s water use?
items.summary:
Protests have arisen in drought-prone US states over water use by AI data centers, which rely on water for cooling processors that generate significant heat. While data centers consumed an estimated 66 billion liters of water in 2023—less than 1% of national use—rapid AI expansion could increase this, especially in water-stressed regions like New Mexico and Arizona.

Researchers note that advances in AI efficiency, liquid cooling technologies, and shifting data centers to water-rich areas with renewable energy can substantially reduce water consumption. Experts suggest that strategic siting and improved cooling methods could cut AI's water footprint by up to 86%, potentially achieving net-zero water use for on-site cooling in the future.

items.title: Google DeepMind pilots world's first double-blind AI evaluations using cryptographic privacy to prevent benchmark contamination [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Piloting the world's first double-blind AI evaluations
items.summary:
Google DeepMind has introduced the first double-blind evaluation of a proprietary AI model, Gemini Flash Lite, using cryptographically secure environments to keep test prompts and model details confidential. This approach prevents benchmark contamination by ensuring neither the model nor evaluators can access each other's sensitive data during testing.

The pilot involves partnerships with the Singapore AI Safety Institute, OpenMined, AVERI, and MLCommons, leveraging Google Cloud's Confidential Computing to protect intellectual property and evaluation data. This method aims to increase trust in AI benchmarks by enabling independent, secure assessments of advanced models without compromising data privacy or security.

This development addresses growing concerns about AI models seeing test questions in advance, which can skew performance results. Double-blind evaluations could become critical for sensitive applications like cybersecurity and government use, setting a new standard for AI model oversight and safety assurance.

The platform includes an observability console to trace and analyze agent activity, providing quality-scored traces and traffic metrics across projects.

Telem's pricing model charges only the upstream provider's per-request rate without additional platform fees for routing, tracing, or analytics. It offers personal plans with full console access and enterprise plans featuring dedicated infrastructure, single sign-on, audit controls, custom integrations, and 24/7 support. The service aims to improve AI agent reliability by managing the interaction layer between agents and the open web, ensuring trustworthy search and fetch operations.

This initiative follows concerns about AI agents hacking systems and misbehaving when controlling physical devices.

The findings suggest that infrastructure orchestration is a critical factor in long-horizon AI performance, shifting the focus from solely model selection to optimizing orchestration layers for better returns on investment in AI deployments.

items.originalTitle: AI Weeds Out Job Applicants with Disabilities, Lawsuit Claims
items.summary:
A federal lawsuit claims that Workday's artificial intelligence hiring tools unfairly screen out job applicants with disabilities, older candidates, and minorities, potentially affecting applicants nationwide. The case, Mobley v. Workday, is being closely watched as Maryland's largest private employer, Johns Hopkins, prepares to transition much of its hiring process to Workday next year.

The lawsuit argues that Workday's AI may introduce bias by favoring traits associated with historically successful employees, while Workday denies intentional discrimination and states its tools focus only on job qualifications with human oversight. Although some claims of intentional discrimination were dismissed, the court allowed claims of disparate impact to proceed. Several local employers using Workday have stated they do not use its AI-driven screening features, highlighting ongoing evaluation of such technologies in recruitment processes.

items.title: Researchers find AI shopping agents give inconsistent product recommendations influenced by source order and memory prompts [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: AI shopping agents aren't ready to buy on your behalf, study finds
items.summary:
Researchers at the Wharton School tested six AI shopping agents and found their product recommendations varied widely based on external information sources, the order of presented sources, and user memory prompts. Even minor changes in context or information sequence caused significant shifts in product choices, with some agents showing up to a 99 percentage point swing in preference.

The study used the ACES simulator to evaluate AI agents selecting fitness watches from a fixed product grid, revealing that a single external source like a Wirecutter review could dramatically influence recommendations. Multiple sources did not stabilize choices, and the order in which sources were presented further affected outcomes. Additionally, user memory statements such as "I love hiking!" shifted selections toward pricier products despite the presence of objectively superior options.

These findings suggest that AI shopping agents currently lack consistency and reliability, making them unsuitable for autonomous purchasing decisions. The variability also poses challenges for sellers trying to optimize for AI-driven shopping, as the agents' decision processes depend on unknown factors including prior information and model-specific behaviors.

items.summary:
A randomized experiment involving more than 1,000 first-year students at Bocconi University examined the effects of ChatGPT access and critical-thinking training on a real-world marketing assignment. Students with ChatGPT access produced higher-quality, more coherent work resembling expert recommendations, while those who received causal reasoning training generated more original ideas. Students who received both interventions showed combined benefits, suggesting that AI tools and critical-thinking skills complement each other in enhancing student performance.

The study used human grading and automated text analysis to evaluate submissions, revealing that traditional grading rubrics may overlook originality and critical reasoning. The findings highlight the need for educational assessments to adapt as AI tools become more prevalent, emphasizing both polished answers and creative, critical thinking. This research contributes to understanding how AI and cognitive training can jointly support student learning outcomes.

items.title: Enterprise AI's real risk isn't autonomous agents. It's the complexity between them. [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Enterprise AI's real risk isn't autonomous agents. It's the complexity between them.
items.summary:
Presented by Gravitee

Agent complexity is the insidious shadow lurking inside enterprises right now that needs a light shone on it.

Thatâs because enterprises don't deploy a single agent and watch it run, they deploy fleets, each one calling APIs, calling other agents, reaching into applications that were never built with a machine decision-maker in mind. That's the failure mode that should keep you up at night: a windy, complicated system nobody can see clearly enough to govern. But why do things get so opaque so quickly?

Add a second agent to a system, and you've added one connection. Add a tenth, and you haven't added ten connections, you've potentially added dozens, because now any agent might call any other, and each of those calls can trigger a call somewhere else. Complexity doesn't creep up with agent headcount. It compounds with the number of paths between agents, and nobody's job is to draw that graph. A support ticket that used to touch one system might now pass through four agents before a human ever lays eyes on it, and every one of those handoffs is a decision point nobody approved.

Most enterprise AI programs stall when the humans responsible for their agents lose the thread. Ask a security team a simple question: which agents can reach which systems, and watch the silence. Ask which agent triggered which downstream action three hops ago. More silence.

The instinct is to treat this like a checklist. Approve the agent. Log the agent. Move on. I'd argue this is the wrong instinct. A checklist checks a single point in time. Complexity runs across a chain, and you can't govern a chain with a stack of one-time approvals any more than you can call a diet successful because you had a vegetable once.

So where does it actually break down?

Permissions creep first. Somebody builds an agent to summarize support tickets, grants it broad API access because scoping it properly would've taken another sprint, and forgets about it. Six months later, that same agent has a path into the payments system. Nobody remembers signing off on that. Nobody did.

And ownership thins out the further the chain runs. Five agents touch one workflow, something breaks at step four, and now you're asking who's responsible for a link nobody was ever assigned to own, because the org chart stopped at "deploy the agent" and never got to "name the human who answers for it."

This is a story about governance infrastructure that hasn't caught up with how agents actually behave: interconnected, cascading, multiplying faster than the processes built to track them.

Fixing the cluster starts with identity. Every agent needs to exist as its own entity, not a shadow permission borrowed from whoever deployed it. Its own name in the register. Its own scoped authority. A named human sponsor who answers for what it does. That part is necessary.

But it is nowhere near sufficient.

The harder piece is the oversight that holds across the entire chain, not just at each individual link in it. You need to see what an agent did, what it set off downstream, and where that trail ends in real time, not in a report someone pulls together once a quarter. Get agent-level identity right and stop there, and you end up with a filing cabinet full of perfectly documented agents operating inside a system nobody can actually explain.

And oversight by itself only tells you what already happened. Watching a chain isn't the same as controlling it. Enforcement is the piece most programs skip: the ability to stop an out-of-policy call before it executes, not just log it for someone to find in a review three weeks later. A dashboard that shows you an agent breached its scope five minutes ago is a monitoring tool. A system that stops the breach from happening in the first place is governance. Enterprises serious about agent accountability need both, and most have only built the first.

We're all running at blazing speed to ensure we're not the ones left behind in the race we've found ourselves in, and we're all too aware that there's a cost to slowing down. Every enterprise serious about agentic AI hits the complexity wall eventually. The ones that get past it are the ones who built enough visibility and accountability, so their fleet can keep growing without anyone losing the ability to answer one question: what is this system doing right now, and who's responsible for it.

But don't miss the point. Complexity isn't a reason to pump the brakes. The enterprises getting this right aren't slowing down. They're building toward Human-Agent Harmony, where scale and accountability grow together instead of trading off against each other.

The real risk was never a single agent doing exactly what it was built to do. It's a hundred of them doing exactly that, all at once, interacting in combinations nobody designed for. That kind of multiplication is what keeps enterprise AI stuck running pilots forever instead of running production.

Solve for complexity and autonomy stops being the villain. It starts being the whole point.

Rory Blundell is CEO at Gravitee.

items.summary:
AI is speeding up chip design. That was a key theme in conversations I had this week with engineers, researchers and a handful of startups pitching AI-driven design help at the annual Hot Chips semiconductor conference in Palo Alto, Calif. 

OpenAI’s Jalapeño chip, which it claims is better than Nvidia’s Blackwell chips at AI inference, is good in part because its Sol and Astra models helped with the design and software process, the OpenAI team said in a presentation. And Google’s tensor processing unit team credited its DeepMind researchers for using AI to help make TPU v8, its latest chips, 6% more power efficient and also 6% more powerful. Nvidia of course has also leaned into AI-driven chip design, with an array of software libraries that apply AI to everything from the stencil layout for how circuits are lasered onto a chip to how data moves between the millions of microscopic parts of a chip.

Design startup Agentrys, which on Wednesday announced it has raised $25 million, aims to help chip designers use AI agents to automate the process and teach chip designs to improve themselves. Its CEO Mark Ren, who led Nvidia’s design automation efforts for the past decade, believes the future of chip design will be driven by “very powerful agentic systems that can do chip design on their own nearly from start to finish,” he said.

items.title: When agents act on their own, governance has to live in the data layer [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
items.originalTitle: When agents act on their own, governance has to live in the data layer
items.summary:
Presented by EDB

As enterprises give AI agents more autonomy â the ability to plan, decide, and act across systems without a human approving each step â a hard question moves to the center of every architecture review: When an agent tries to complete an action that it was never authorized to do, what actually stops it?

These are your agents, running on your models, touching your data in your infrastructure â and the responsibility for what they do sits with you. That responsibility canât be met in hindsight or with a set of abstract policies that live on paper but not in practice. Agents need rules in the context of the moment, because they donât exercise overriding judgment of their own actions.

Consider a simple rule: Never open the car door. Followed literally, an agent could never get in or out of the car at all. But if you change the context (the car has just crashed, thereâs a fire, someone is hurt and needs to get out), then the rule you actually want is the opposite. Context in the moment is everything. We are asking agents to do intelligent things; that requires intelligent rules.

The instinct is to add guardrails around the agent: instructions, policies, and monitoring layered above the model. Those mechanisms matter, but they share a structural limit: The car-door rule is plausible right up until the moment you actually have to decide whether to open the door. Controls at the agent layer are only as reliable as the agentâs output is predictable, and autonomy is precisely the property that makes that output hard to predict. Governance that depends on reviewing an action before it happens cannot keep pace with a system that acts in milliseconds, across many systems at once.

Governance has to become executable, and enforced where agents actually do their work: at the operational data layer, in the context, and exactly at the moment it is happening.

The data layer is the enforcement point

Agents create value by touching data. They query it, retrieve it, transform it, and increasingly act on it. A policy that says an agent should not reach a certain class of data is meaningful only if the system can deny that access at the moment the agent requests it. Additionally, a principle that says AI must be auditable is meaningful only if the organization can reconstruct what the agent did, what data it touched, which user it acted for, and what resulted. When governance lives at the data layer, it holds regardless of how the agent was built or how it behaves, because the control is a property of the database itself, not a promise made by the agent.

Agent behavior may be probabilistic. Governance cannot be

The enterprise should not rely on a model choosing to follow policy. The policy has to be enforced by the system. That is the difference between hoping an actor stays in bounds and constructing bounds it cannot cross to begin with.

The controls that make this real are ones many enterprises already run at the data layer: role- and attribute-based access, row- and column-level security, classification and masking, policy as code, and complete audit trails.

What agents change is not the mechanism, but who the mechanism has to recognize. Identity management has to treat the agent as a principal in its own right, with its own identity and a purpose declared when the session opens.

Once purpose is bound to identity, the policy engine can evaluate it the same way it evaluates role or department today, and the record of what happened can capture not just who acted and what they touched, but what they declared they were there to do.

In practice, this resolves into nine controls, grouped under three imperatives:

Enforce it

  • Role- and attribute-based access control enforced at query time, for agents as well as users

  • Dynamic column masking driven by the same policy path

  • Agent identity as a first-class principal, with declared purpose bound at session start and the acting user preserved

See it and prove it

  • Classification and tagging that drives policy

  • Session-level audit logging that records which agent acted, for which user, and under what declared purpose

  • Lineage across pipelines, so a result can be traced back to the request that produced it

Unify and harden

  • Centralized, portable policy management

  • Encryption at rest and in transit

  • Consistent enforcement across on-prem, cloud, and sovereign or air-gapped environments

âDeclared purpose is what makes the difference. It becomes an attribute the access layer already understands, evaluated in the same policy path as role and row-level security. The enforcement mechanism does not change. What changes is that the agent's purpose is part of what it evaluates, and part of what the record proves afterward,â says Priyanka Jain, VP, product management, data & AI governance, EDB.

Wherever you are in your AI adoption journey, enforcement at the data layer is what lets you move faster rather than slower. The controls are already in the database. The difference is that agents now have to pass through them.

A digital leash, not a locked door

The goal is not to stop agents from doing useful work. It is to define how far an agent can go, what it can touch, what it can change, what requires escalation, and how the organization can reconstruct events if something goes wrong. Governed this way, agents are identified, scoped, monitored, and auditable. The enterprise can adopt them faster, because security, risk, and leadership teams trust the operating model underneath.

Open, sovereign, and enforceable at the source

Built on open source Postgres, this open foundation keeps enterprises in control of where their data lives, who can reach it, and under what policy, without ceding governance to a layer they donât own or canât inspect. For regulated industries, that combination of data sovereignty and source-level enforcement isnât a nice-to-have; itâs the precondition for putting agents into production at all.

Agentic systems will keep getting more capable and more autonomous. That is a reason to be deliberate about where control lives, not a reason to slow down. The enterprises that enforce governance at the data layer can move aggressively on AI, because the thing protecting their data is more than just wishful thinking.

items.summary:
Nvidia has agreed to buy Hugging Face, a company known for its GitHub-like repository of open-source AI models, for $12.9 billion, according to a person with knowledge of the agreement.

The move will put Nvidia in charge of a strategic asset in the race among open-source model developers to catch up to closed-source AI models from Anthropic and OpenAI. Nvidia leaders believe that a plethora of successful open models will help preserve its AI hardware dominance because they will be a counterweight to the closed-source AI developers, each of which is trying to develop competing AI server chips and lessen their reliance on Nvidia’s.
